chapter_map.summary_en: Describes the conduction system from sinus node to Purkinje network and the cell physiology underneath it: resting and action potentials and how each phase maps onto the QRS, ST and T, fast- versus slow-response cells, and refractory periods. Ends with dipole theory, which explains why an electrode records a positive, negative or equiphasic deflection.

Covers the electrocardiograph, paper and calibration, the bipolar, augmented and chest lead systems (including right-sided, posterior and Medrano leads), recording technique and electrode colours. Defines wave names, intervals, QT correction and Bailey's reference systems, and gives norm tables by age and heart rate.

Builds the normal tracing from atrial, AV-junctional and three-vector ventricular activation, then covers heart position and rotation, normal repolarization and its variants, and the paediatric ECG. Closes with the book's six-step reading method: rhythm, rate, PR, QT, axis and morphology.

chapter_map.title_es: El electrocardiograma en los crecimientos atriales
chapter_map.summary_en: Derives right, left and biatrial enlargement from when each atrium is activated within the P wave. Gives criteria for axis, height, duration, V1 polarity and indirect QRS signs, and explains how coarse f waves in atrial fibrillation point to a large left atrium.

chapter_map.title_es: El electrocardiograma en los crecimientos ventriculares
chapter_map.summary_en: Explains LVH and RVH as enlarged activation vectors: axis shift, voltage indices, intrinsicoid deflection, transition shift and overload repolarization. Includes the Romhilt-Estes and Flowers-Horan scores, the conditions that mask hypertrophy, and the ECG in pulmonary embolism and cor pulmonale.

chapter_map.title_es: El electrocardiograma en los bloqueos de rama y bloqueos fasciculares
chapter_map.title_en: The ECG in bundle branch and fascicular blocks
chapter_map.summary_en: Uses the intraseptal barrier and a slow transseptal vector to derive complete and incomplete RBBB and LBBB, and reads fascicular blocks in the frontal plane. Also covers bi- and trifascicular, rate-dependent and masked block, Brugada syndrome and the prognosis of each block.

Classifies AV block by degree and by site (His-bundle intervals) and gives surface criteria for first-degree, Mobitz I and II, fixed, variable, advanced and complete block. Explains the arithmetic of Wenckebach cycles and how the escape QRS shows where the block sits.

chapter_map.title_es: El electrocardiograma en los síndromes de preexcitación
chapter_map.summary_en: Defines WPW, LGL, Mahaim and concealed pathways and explains how fusion sets the degree of pre-excitation. Covers pathway localization from delta polarity, the patterns WPW can mimic, orthodromic and antidromic reentry, pre-excited AF, risk markers and the ECG after ablation.

chapter_map.title_es: El electrocardiograma en la cardiopatía isquémica
chapter_map.title_en: The ECG in ischaemic heart disease
chapter_map.summary_en: Sorts coronary ECG changes into ischaemia (T), injury (ST) and necrosis (Q), each subendocardial or subepicardial, and follows their time course and lead territories. Covers non-Q, posterior and RV infarction, Prinzmetal angina, silent ischaemia, aneurysm, signs of reperfusion and how to identify the culprit artery.

chapter_map.title_es: Prueba de esfuerzo y tests farmacológicos
chapter_map.title_en: Exercise stress testing and pharmacological tests
chapter_map.summary_en: Covers exercise physiology, test protocols, target heart rate and lead systems, then ischaemic ST criteria, blood-pressure, arrhythmia and conduction responses, functional capacity and the Duke score. Also lists contraindications, stopping criteria, false results, Bayesian reasoning and radionuclide and drug stress tests.

chapter_map.title_es: El electrocardiograma en las cardiopatías congénitas
chapter_map.title_en: The ECG in congenital heart disease
chapter_map.summary_en: Sets paediatric norms and reads each lesion by the pressure or volume load it puts on each chamber. Covers cyanotic lesions (tricuspid atresia, pulmonary atresia, critical PS, Ebstein, TGA, TAPVC, truncus, DORV) and acyanotic ones (ASD, VSD, PDA, AVSD, AS, PS, coarctation, HCM).

chapter_map.summary_en: Introduces pacing electrophysiology (Ohm's law, energy, threshold, impedance, lead polarity) and the pacing modes with their timing cycles and special algorithms. Gives pacing indications for each conduction disorder and describes follow-up, including the expected paced QRS and the magnet response.

Classifies the arrhythmias and defines sinus rhythm, including P-axis variants. Then covers sinus arrhythmia, pauses, sick sinus syndrome, wandering pacemaker, atrial premature beats, paroxysmal, blocked and multifocal atrial tachycardia, flutter, fibrillation and atrial dissociation.

chapter_map.title_es: Arritmias del tejido de la unión
chapter_map.summary_en: Separates passive junctional rhythms and escape beats from active junctional premature beats and tachycardia. Explains where the retrograde P falls, the dual-pathway AV nodal reentry with its pseudo-r' and pseudo-s, and complete, incomplete and isorhythmic AV dissociation.

Covers PVCs (coupling, pause, morphology, grouping, R-on-T, Lown grade) and how to tell them from aberrancy, plus escape and idioventricular rhythms. Then VT with dissociation, capture and fusion beats, the approach to wide-QRS tachycardia including the Brugada algorithm, accelerated idioventricular rhythm, torsades, and ventricular flutter and fibrillation.
An alphabetical topic-to-page index, used here to confirm where each chapter starts and ends. PDF 299 is the back cover.

reading_method: 1. Context first: note the patient's age, sex, symptoms and drugs (digitalis, antiarrhythmics, beta-blockers), and find any previous ECG to compare. Always read all 12 leads together, never a single lead.

2. Technical check: the calibration pulse should be 10 mm per mV with square corners (rescale if the gain is half or double). Paper speed should be 25 mm/s (1 mm = 0.04 s). Check for a stable baseline, correct electrode colours and positions, and that II = I + III. P positive in aVR or negative in I suggests swapped arm cables.

3. Rhythm: is it sinus? Look for a normal P before every QRS (negative in aVR, positive in II, +/- in V1), a constant PR of at least 0.12 s, regular RR (spread ≤0.16 s) and a rate of 60-100 bpm. If not, find where the atrial activity starts.

4. Rate: for a regular rhythm, divide 300 by the number of large squares between R waves. For an irregular rhythm, count QRS complexes in 6 s and multiply by 10. Compare with the norms for age, and measure atrial and ventricular rates separately when they differ.

5. P wave in II and V1: normal is ≤0.10 s, ≤2.5 mm, axis about +54°. A tall peaked P with ++- in V1 suggests right atrial enlargement. A wide notched P with +-- in V1 suggests left atrial enlargement.

6. PR: measure from the start of P to the start of QRS and judge it against age and rate. A short PR calls for a search for a delta wave (WPW), LGL or a junctional or low atrial origin. A long PR means first-degree block. If P waves are dropped, march them out and classify the second- or third-degree block.
7. QRS: normal width is 0.06-0.10 s. At 0.12 s or more, consider bundle branch block (compare V1-V2 with V5-V6), pre-excitation or a ventricular origin. Name each complex (rS, qR, rsR', QS).

8. Frontal axis: use the hexaxial system, either with the net QRS of I and III or with the isodiphasic lead. Compare with the age range. Marked deviation suggests a fascicular block, hypertrophy or heart position. If every limb lead is isodiphasic, the axis is indeterminate.
9. Precordial progression: expect rS in V1-V2, transition at V3-V4 and qRs in V5-V6. A shifted transition points to rotation, hypertrophy or infarction.
10. Chambers: use age-adjusted voltages and indices (Sokolow, Lewis, Cabrera), the intrinsicoid deflection, the transition and overload repolarization, plus point scores and the clinical context.
11. Q waves: separate a small septal q from a pathological Q (more than 25% of R and/or at least 0.04 s, notched). Group the leads with Q waves to localise necrosis.

12. ST: measure at the J point against the PR baseline. Map elevation or depression to a coronary territory and look for reciprocal changes. In inferior MI, compare III with II, check I and aVL, and record V3R-V4R. In V1-V2, tall R with ST depression may be posterior MI.

13. T and U: T normally has the same polarity as the main QRS (negative in aVR). Symmetric pointed inversion suggests ischaemia; asymmetric inversion opposite to the QRS suggests overload or BBB. Tall peaked T is also abnormal. Apply the normal variants for age, sex and ethnicity, and look for a U wave.
14. QT: measure from QRS onset to the end of T and correct for rate (Bazett QTc ≤0.44 s, or predicted QT = 0.39 × √RR). Watch for T-U fusion.
15. Confounders: BBB, pre-excitation, LVH strain, digitalis and pacing all produce secondary ST-T changes, so do not use ischaemia criteria on them.

16. Arrhythmia subroutines. Pause: compare it with the PP cycle and search the preceding T for a blocked P'. Extra beat: decide early or late, look for a preceding P', and assess QRS width, coupling and the pause. Narrow tachycardia: locate the P relative to the QRS and look for F or f waves (a vagal manoeuvre helps). Wide tachycardia: apply the stepwise VT algorithm and look for dissociation, capture and fusion beats.
17. Paced ECG: identify the spikes, the paced chamber, capture and sensing, the timing intervals, and the expected LBBB-like paced QRS with a superior axis.
18. Synthesis: list the findings in order (rhythm, rate, conduction, axis, chambers, ischaemia), compare with the earlier tracing, and answer the clinical question.

exercise_ideas.idea: Calibration and paper-speed trap: before measuring anything, the learner must work out the gain and speed from the calibration pulse and tick marks.
Electrode-placement torso drill covering standard, posterior, right-sided, Medrano and exercise positions, showing how misplacement changes the ECG.
Dipole sandbox: drag an electrode around a moving wavefront and watch the deflection change sign.
Hexaxial axis lab: rotate the QRS vector and watch all six limb leads update, then reverse the task and drag the vector to match six given leads.
Caliper drill for PR, QRS, QT and QTc, including a case with T-U fusion.
Heart-rate trainer comparing the 300 rule with a 6-second count on regular strips and on AF.
Atrial-size sliders that redraw the P wave in lead II and V1 as each atrium grows.
Wall-thickness sliders with live voltage indices and score builders (Sokolow, Lewis, Cabrera, Romhilt-Estes).
Block builder: cut a branch or fascicle and see the resulting 12-lead ECG.
Wenckebach ladder-diagram simulator with an atypical-form toggle.
March-out-the-P-waves tool for complete AV block and AV dissociation.
Pause analyser that sorts each pause into sinus arrest, SA block or blocked PAC.
Infarct time slider showing how ST, Q and T evolve from minutes to a month.
Two-way territory map: from leads to coronary territory and back, with reciprocal changes and RCA-versus-circumflex reasoning.
LAD occlusion-site simulator based on the Engelen patterns.
Virtual stress lab: measure ST at J+80 ms, decide when to stop the test, and calculate the Duke score.
Pre-excitation fusion slider plus pathway localisation using the Arruda algorithm.
Vagal-manoeuvre button that unmasks flutter or AF waves or terminates AVNRT.
Step-by-step Brugada algorithm on wide-QRS tachycardias, with hunts for capture and fusion beats.
Age slider showing the normal ECG from newborn to adult.
Pacemaker timing sandbox to classify capture and sensing.

pitfalls: Check the calibration pulse and paper speed before taking any measurement.
Check that II = I + III. P positive in aVR suggests swapped arm cables.
Never read a single lead in isolation.
The normal PR range depends on heart rate and age.
QT must be corrected for heart rate, and T-U fusion makes the end of T hard to find.
Negative T waves in V1-V4 can be normal in children and some women.
Applying adult criteria to children leads to over-diagnosis.
Right atrial enlargement makes the P wave taller, not wider.
Sensitivity for LVH is only about 50%.
A tall R in V1 has a differential: RVH, RBBB, posterior MI, WPW.
The book gives both ≥0.12 s and >0.12 s as the BBB cut-off; fix one rule.
Fascicular blocks keep the QRS narrow.
An RBBB-like V1 with persistent ST elevation should raise suspicion of Brugada syndrome.
P waves hidden in T waves are easily missed.
A 2:1 block cannot be typed as Mobitz I or II from one strip.
A late wide beat after a pause is an escape beat, not a PVC.
AV dissociation is not the same as complete AV block.
A small septal q wave is not a pathological Q wave.
ST depression opposite a STEMI is reciprocal, not a second infarct.
Look for RV involvement in every inferior MI.
Posterior MI appears only as a mirror image in V1-V2.
ST changes are not interpretable with LBBB, WPW or digitalis.
A negative exercise test below the target heart rate is inconclusive, not normal.
A normal ECG does not exclude an accessory pathway.
WPW can mimic infarction, hypertrophy or BBB.
Flutter with 2:1 conduction at about 150 bpm is easily missed.
Fast AF can look regular.
Treat a wide-QRS tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise.
Measure the QT before calling a rhythm torsades.
Paced QRS complexes look like LBBB.
Source inconsistencies across chapters: Sokolow lead, LBBB axis range, LAFB axis range, the 'PR 24 ms' erratum.
